questions.text:
Consider the following statements regarding the front-end and back-end of a compiler.

S1: The front-end includes phases that are independent of the target hardware.
S2: The back-end includes phases that are specific to the target hardware.
S3: The back-end includes phases that are specific to the programming language used in the source code.

Identify the CORRECT option.
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Front end (lexical, syntax, semantic analysis, intermediate code) depends on the source language, not on the target machine [latex]\text{---}[/latex] S1 TRUE.
- Back end (code optimization for the machine, code generation) is specific to the target hardware [latex]\text{---}[/latex] S2 TRUE.
- The back end works on intermediate code, so it is independent of the source language [latex]\text{---}[/latex] S3 FALSE.

Answer: Only S1 and S2 are TRUE

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Only S1 and S2 are TRUE.
S1, S2, and S3 are all TRUE.
Only S1 and S3 are TRUE.

questions.text:
Consider the following grammar along with translation rules.
[latex] \begin{aligned} &S \rightarrow S_1 \# T & & \{S._{val}=S_{1.val}*T._{val} \} \\ &S \rightarrow T & & \{S._{val}=T._{val} \} \\ &T \rightarrow T_1 \% R & & \{T._{val}=T_{1.val} \div R._{val} \} \\ &T \rightarrow R & & \{T._{val}=R._{val} \} \\ &R \rightarrow id & & \{R._{val}=id._{val} \} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Here [latex] \#[/latex] and [latex] \%[/latex] are operators and [latex]id[/latex] is a token that represents an integer and [latex]id_{.val}[/latex] represents the corresponding integer value. The set of non-terminals is [latex] \{S,T,R,P \}[/latex] and a subscripted non-terminal indicates an instance of the non-terminal.
Using this translation scheme, the computed value of [latex]S_{.val}[/latex] for root of the parse tree for the expression [latex]20 \# 10 \% 5 \# 8 \% 2 \% 2[/latex] is
questions.solution:
From the grammar, # (multiply) is at the S level, so it has lower precedence; % (divide) is at the T level, so it binds tighter. Both are left recursive, i.e. left associative.

[latex]20\,\#\,(10\%5)\,\#\,((8\%2)\%2)=20\times2\times2=80[/latex]

Answer: 80

questions.text:
Consider the augmented grammar with [latex] \{+, *, (, ), id \}[/latex] as the set of terminals.
[latex] \begin{aligned}&S' \rightarrow S \\ &S \rightarrow S+R|R \\ &R \rightarrow R*P|P \\ &P \rightarrow (S)|id \end{aligned}[/latex]
If [latex]I_0[/latex] is the set of two [latex]LR(0)[/latex] items [latex] \{ [S' \rightarrow S.], [S \rightarrow S.+R] \}[/latex], then [latex]goto(closure(I_0 ),+)[/latex] contains exactly ______ items.
questions.solution:
Closure of [latex]I_0[/latex] adds nothing (the dot is before + and at the end, not before a non-terminal).

goto on +: [latex]S\rightarrow S+.R[/latex]. Closure (dot before R, then before P):
1. [latex]S\rightarrow S+.R[/latex]
2. [latex]R\rightarrow .R*P[/latex]
3. [latex]R\rightarrow .P[/latex]
4. [latex]P\rightarrow .(S)[/latex]
5. [latex]P\rightarrow .id[/latex]

Answer: 5

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.text: Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- LALR(1) merges LR(1) states with the same core; this merging can create a new reduce-reduce conflict [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- The symbol table is used in almost every phase (semantic analysis, code generation, [latex]\ldots[/latex]) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Data flow analysis is used for code optimization, not run-time memory management [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Every deterministic CFL has an LR(1) grammar, so LR(1) parsing is sufficient for DCFLs [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: LR(1) parsing is sufficient for deterministic context-free languages

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options:
The LALR(1) parser for a grammar G cannot have reduce-reduce conflict if the
LR(1) parser for G does not have reduce-reduce conflict.
Symbol table is accessed only during the lexical analysis phase.
Data flow analysis is necessary for run-time memory management.
LR(1) parsing is sufficient for deterministic context-free languages.

questions.text:
Consider the following augmented grammar with [latex]\{ \#, @, <, >, a, b, c \}[/latex] as the set of terminals.

[latex]\begin{array}{l} S' \rightarrow S \\ S \rightarrow S \# cS \\ S \rightarrow SS \\ S \rightarrow S @ \\ S \rightarrow < S > \\ S \rightarrow a \\ S \rightarrow b \\ S \rightarrow c \end{array}[/latex]

Let [latex]I_0 = \text{CLOSURE}(\{S' \rightarrow \bullet S\})[/latex]. The number of items in the set [latex]\text{GOTO(GOTO}(I_0 \lt ), \lt )[/latex] is ___________
questions.solution:
In [latex]I_0[/latex], [latex]S\rightarrow\bullet\lt S\gt[/latex] moves on [latex]\lt[/latex] to [latex]S\rightarrow\lt\bullet S\gt[/latex], and its closure adds all 7 S-items with the dot at the start: 1 + 7 = 8 items.

Doing GOTO on [latex]\lt[/latex] again (from [latex]S\rightarrow\bullet\lt S\gt[/latex] inside that set) gives the same set again: 8 items.

Answer: 8
